Gwalior Bench: Dated 16/10/2020  Shri Anand Mohan Mathur, learned senior counsel assisted by Shri Abhinav Dhanodkar, Shri Vaibhav Asawa and Shri Manas Dubey, learned counsel for the petitioner.
 Shri Nitin Goyal, learned PL for the respondent/State.

With consent heard on the point on admission through Video Conferencing.
The instant petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. is being preferred for quashment of FIR registered vide No. 32/2020 dated 24/1/2020 at Police Station Purani Chhawani, District Gwalior for offence registered under Section 274 of IPC, Section 27 of Drugs and Cosmetic Act, 1940 and Section 13 of Drugs Control Act, 1950.

Precisely stated facts of the case are that petitioner possess two licences, one licence under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 bearing licence No. 11419570000049 on the registered address Kelax Health Care, Saint John Vinni School, Purani Chhawani and the second licence bearing No.
20B/195/57/2016, which is a licence to sell, stock or exhibit or offer for sale, or distribute by whole sale drugs other than specified in (Schedule C, C(1) and X) on the address Goverdhan Colony, Bhind Road, District Gwalior.
It appears that on 24/1/2020 around 12.30 pm Drugs HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) Inspector, Food and Drugs Department, State of Madhya Pradesh,
District Gwalior (respondent No. 2) conducted a sudden inspection at the premises of present petitioner and found some packaging material, Machinery related to manufacturing of drugs,
unlabelled bottles and adulterated drugs at the premises, therefore Drugs Inspector lodged the FIR against the present petitioner and other co-accused persons for offence referred above.

sentences.text: Respondent No. 2 with the help of other authorities conducted this raid on petitioner's premises under his authority and arrested Manish Joshi and Rahul Dubey, who were present on the spot but another co-accused Udal Singh Bhadauriya, who was also present on the spot could not be arrested and apparently he fled away.

It further appears that respondent No. 2 being the authority under the Drugs and Cosmetic Act,
1940 (for short "Act of 1940"), therefore, filed the complaint under the provisions of Section 18 (c)
which is punishable under Section 27 (b) (ii) of Act of 1940 and since the offence is repeated Sanjay Pathak vs The State Of M.P. on 16 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116750914/
1 therefore, it is punishable under Section 30 (1) (a) of Act of 1940 also.

sentences.text: It is the submission of learned senior counsel for the petitioner that alleged adulterated / expired drugs do not belong to petitioner.
In fact it belongs to one Alok Mishra, who filed an application under Section 451 and 457 of Cr.P.C. to claim those drugs which were found in the premises of petitioner.

According to Alok Mishra, drugs belonged to him and he sent those drugs in an auto rickshaw for placing those drugs in a pit in some remote area but auto which carried the drugs got some problem and therefore, as a stop gap arrangement, those expired drugs were kept in the premises of petitioner and therefore those drugs never belonged to the petitioner.

Another ground raised by petitioner is regarding jurisdiction and competence as according to learned senior counsel, complaint can only be filed by Drugs Inspector under Section 190-200 of Cr.P.C. and not by police and here FIR has been registered at the instance of police officer and thereafter charge-sheet has been filed, therefore, same is without authority.

In support of his submissions, he relied upon decision of Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Union of India Vs. Ashok Kuamr HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) Sharma and Ors.
2020 SCC Online SC 683.

It is further submitted that Section 274 of IPC is a cognizable offence and except on complaint,
cognizance cannot be taken.
He referred the representation preferred by wife of petitioner to submit that false case has been prepared against her husband.

Petitioner being innocent has been falsely implicated, therefore, his case be considered in light of submissions made above and petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. be allowed and case registered against the petitioner be quashed.

Per contra, learned Panel Lawyer appearing on behalf of respondents/State opposed the prayer and submits that as per notification dated 19/2/2008, respondent No. 2-Drugs Inspector has been notified as Inspector as per Section 21 of the Act of 1940 and he has authority to file complaint and in the instant case complaint has been filed, therefore, no legal impairment exists qua present case.
Looking to the contents of complaint, sufficient case is made out for trial.

Petitioner is still absconding, therefore, case has been filed in his absence and he is not cooperating in HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) investigation as well as in trial.

sentences.text: He prayed for dismissal of the petition.
Heard the counsel for the parties at length and perused the case diary.

This is a case, where, petitioner is seeking quashment of case registered against him purportedly for offence under Section 27 of Act of 1940 and Section 13 of the Act of 1950 alongwith Section 274 of IPC.

So far as the point regarding maintainability of the case against the petitioner is concerned, perusal of case diary indicates that on 24/1/2020, Ajay Thakur, Drugs Inspector under Food and Drugs Sanjay Pathak vs The State Of M.P. on 16 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116750914/
2 Administration inspected the premises of petitioner and found several manufacturing machines for manufacturing drugs, some expired and adulterated drugs, unlabeled bottles, chemicals / raw material used for manufacturing of drugs and several other articles as referred in seizure memo were seized alongwith cartons, expired diclofenac gel, albendazole suspension etc.

Ajay Thakur, who is working as Drugs Inspector in Food and Drugs Administration has been notified vide notification dated 19/2/2008 as Drugs Inspector for the whole of State of Madhya Pradesh as per Section 21 of the Act of 1940.
HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)

entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: It is further revealed from the case diary that after raid being conducted over the premises of petitioner, Manish Joshi and Rahul Dubey and Udal Singh Bhadauriya were present but Manish Joshi and Rahul Dubey were arrested and it further appears that Udal Singh and present petitioner are still absconding.
Seizure memo was prepared and all procedures in accordance with law were undertaken.

In fact, a complaint has been filed by the Drugs Inspector against the accused persons and therefore,
contention of learned senior counsel for the petitioner sans merits regarding authority and jurisdiction because respondent No. 2 was well within his authority to file complaint and any police officer (or Investigating Officer for that matter) has not filed the charge-sheet as tried to be projected by learned senior counsel for the petitioner.
Apex Court in the case of H.N.Rishbud Vs. State of Delhi, AIR 1955 SC 196, has considered this aspect and held in para 9 as under:-
"9.The question then requires to be considered whether and to what extent the trial which follows such investigation is vitiated.

entities.text: H.N.Rishbud Vs. State of Delhi, AIR 1955 SC 196
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Now, trial follows cognizance and cognizance is preceded by investigation.
This is undoubtedly the basic scheme of the Code in respect of cognizable cases.
But it HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) does not necessarily follow that an invalid investigation nullifies the cognizance or trial based thereon.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Here we are not concerned with the effect of the breach of a mandatory provision regulating the competence or procedure of the Court as regards cognizance or trial.
It is only with reference to such a breach that the question as to whether it constitutes an illegality vitiating the proceedings or a mere irregularity arises.
A defect or illegality in investigation, however serious, has no direct bearing on the competence or the procedure relating to cognizance or trial.
No doubt a police report which results from an investigation is provided in Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the material on which cognizance is taken.
But it cannot be maintained that a valid and legal police report is the foundation of the jurisdiction of the Court to take cognizance.
Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is one out of a group of sections under the heading "Conditions requisite for initiation of proceedings".
The language of this section is in marked contrast with that of the other sections of the group under the same heading, i.e. Section 193 and 195 to 199.
These latter sections regulate the competence of the Court and bar its jurisdiction in certain cases excepting in compliance therewith.
But Section 190 does not.

While no doubt, in one Sanjay Pathak vs The State Of M.P. on 16 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116750914/
3 HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) sense,
clauses (a), (b) and (c) of Section 190 (1) are conditions requisite for taking of cognizance, it is not possible to say that cognizance on an invalid police report is prohibited and is therefore a nullity.

entities.text: Sanjay Pathak vs The State Of M.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Such an invalid report may still fall either under clause (a) or (b) of Section 190 (1), (whether it is the one or the other we need not pause to consider) and in any case cognizance so taken is only in the nature of error in a proceeding antecedent to the trial.

To such a situation section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which is in the following terms is attracted:
"Subject to the provisions herein before contained, no finding, sentence or order passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction shall be reversed or altered on appeal or revision on account of any error, omission or irregularity in the complaint, summons,
warrant, charge, proclamation, order, judgment or other proceedings before or during trial or in any enquiry or other proceedings under this Code, unless such error, omission or irregularity, has in fact occasioned a failure of justice".

If, therefore, cognizance is in fact taken, on a police report vitiated by the breach of a mandatory provision relating to investigation, there can be no doubt that the result of the trial which follows it cannot be set aside unless the illegality in the HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) investigation can be shown to have brought about a miscarriage of justice.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
That an illegality committed in the course of investigation does not affect the competence and the jurisdiction of the Court for trial is well settled as appears from the cases in Prabhu vs. Emperor,
(1861) 30 LJ Ch 379 and Lumbhardar Zutshi Vs. The King, Criminal Appeals Nos 25-D and 434 of 1953 disposed of on 3rd May, 1954.

entities.text: Lumbhardar Zutshi Vs. The King, Criminal Appeals Nos 25-D and 434 of 1953
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: These no doubt relate to the illegality of arrest in the course of investigation while we are concerned in the present cases with the illegality with reference to the machinery for the collection of the evidence.

This distinction may have a bearing on the question of prejudice or miscarriage of justice, but both the cases clearly show that invalidity of the investigation has no relation to the competence of the Court.

We are, therefore, clearly, also, of the opinion that where the cognizance of the case has in fact been taken and the case has proceeded to termination.,
the invalidity of the precedent investigation does not vitiate the result, unless miscarriage of justice has been caused thereby."

Said judgment of Apex Court still holds the field and has been referred in judgment of Apex Court in the case of Vinubhai Haribhai Malviya andOrs. Vs. State of Gujrat and Anr.,2019 SCC Online SC 1346 and the judgment rendered in the case of HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) Ashok Kukmar Sharma (supra) as relied upon by the petitioner.

entities.text: Vinubhai Haribhai Malviya andOrs. Vs. State of Gujrat and Anr.,2019 SCC Online SC 1346
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) Ashok Kukmar Sharma
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
Conclusions drawn by Apex Court in the case of Ashok Kumar Sharma (supra) are reproduced for ready reference:-
"162.

Thus, we may cull out our conclusions/directions as follows:
I.

In regard to cognizable offences under Chapter IV of the Act, in view of Section 32 of the Act and also the scheme of the Cr.P.C., the Police Officer cannot prosecute Sanjay Pathak vs The State Of M.P. on 16 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116750914/
4 offenders in regard to such offences.

entities.text: Sanjay Pathak vs The State Of M.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Only the persons mentioned in Section 32 are entitled to do the same.

II. There is no bar to the Police Officer, however, to investigate and prosecute the person where he has committed an offence, as stated under Section 32 (3)of the Act, i.e., if he has committed any cognizable offence under any other law.

III. Having regard to the scheme of the Cr.P.C. and also the mandate of Section 32 of the Act and on a conspectus of powers which are available with the Drugs Inspector under the Act and also his duties, a Police Officer cannot register a FIR under Section 154 of the CrPC, in regard to cognizable offences under Chapter IV of the Act and he cannot investigate such offences under the provisions of the Cr.P.C.
IV.

Having regard to the provisions of Section 22 (1) (d) of the Act, we hold that an arrest can be HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) made by the Drugs Inspector in regard to cognizable offences falling under Chapter IV of the Act without any warrant and otherwise treating it as a cognizable offence.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
He is, however, bound by the law as laid down in D.K. Basu (supra) and to follow the provisions of Cr.P.C.
V.

It would appear that on the understanding that the Police Officer can register a FIR, there are many cases where FIRs have been registered in regard to cognizable offences falling under Chapter IV of the Act.

We find substance in the stand taken by learned Amicus Curiae and direct that they should be made over to the Drugs Inspectors, if not already made over, and it is for the Drugs Inspector to take action on the same in accordance with the law.
We must record that we are resorting to our power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India in this regard.

VI. Further, we would be inclined to believe that in a number of cases on the understanding of the law relating to the power of arrest as, in fact, evidenced by the facts of the present case, police officers would have made arrests in regard to offences under Chapter IV of the Act.

Therefore, in regard to the power of arrest, we make it clear that our decision that Police Officers do not have power to arrest in respect of cognizable offences HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
under Chapter IV of the Act, will operate with effect from the date of this Judgment.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: VII. We further direct that the Drugs Inspectors, who carry out the arrest, must not only report the arrests, as provided in Section 58 of the CrPC, but also immediately report the arrests to their superior Officers."

Perusal of all these judgments specially the judgment relied by learned senior counsel for the petitioner in the case of Ashok Kumar Sharma (supra), it appears that nowhere the complaint filed by the Drugs Inspector is barred and here the complaint has been filed by the Drugs Inspector and even if any anomaly exists, that has been taken care of in Clause V of para 162 (conclusions /directions).
Therefore, contentions of petitioner lacks merits so far as his argument regarding jurisdiction is concerned.
No miscarriage of justice has been caused to the petitioner, who is otherwise not cooperating with administration of justice.

sentences.text: Perusal of factual matrix reveals that petitioner under the garb of licence taken for preparation of Food Items was manufacturing adulterated drugs or drugs without licence or selling expired drugs without any licence.

In year 2019 also he was found manufacturing drugs without licence and therefore, on HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) 30/9/2019,
his premises was raided and medicines were confiscated.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Therefore, this is his repeat offence.
Beside that, seizure memo and statement of different witnesses and other documents indicate that sufficient material exists against the petitioner to go for trial.

So far as submissions regarding application under Section 451/457 of Cr.P.C. is concerned, it is an eyewash and a screen tried to be created by the petitioner to get rid of charges somehow and therefore, such doubtful defence prima facie cannot be looked into at this juncture while considering a petition for quashment under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. which is an extraordinary jurisdiction and has to be exercised sparingly.
Instant case is not such case where facts are such stream lined or the case is without any factual dichotomy so as to exercise the extraordinary jurisdiction.
Therefore, on this count also, petition lacks merits.

One surprising aspect in the case is that petitioner is still absconding for last almost nine months alongwith another co- accused Udal Singh Bhadauriya, who was although present on spot but later on fled away and after so many months, petitioner has; not only filed this petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. but also anticipatory bail application under Section 438 of Cr.P.C.
HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.) vide M.Cr.C.No.
34641/2020 that too apparently when this Court expressed surprise over the conduct of police officers while granting temporary bail under Section 439 Cr.P.C. to other co- accused Manish Joshi and Rahul Dubey vide order dated 1/9/2020 in M.Cr.C. Nos. 16078/2020 and 14611/2020 respectively and asked the report of concerned Police Officer (SHO) about the steps taken in this regard.

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH (Sanjay Pathak Vs. State of M.P.)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Therefore, petitioner is trying to take the benefit of Rule of law and Administration of Justice without showing due respect and cooperation for the same.

If the case of the petitioner is tested on the touchstone of parameters given by the Apex Court in the case of State of Haryana and others Vs. Ch. Bhajan Lal and others, AIR 1992 SC 604, then it appears that none of the parameters is attracted in the present set of facts.

entities.text: State of Haryana and others Vs. Ch. Bhajan Lal and others, AIR 1992 SC 604
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Cumulatively, petition sans merits and is hereby dismissed.
Petitioner has to participate in trial by submitting before the course of justice and would be at liberty to raise all the grounds available to him in accordance with law.
Trial Court be informed accordingly.

(Anand Pathak) Judge jps/-
